claim: DNA topoisomerase VI (topo VI) is a type IIB DNA topoisomerase found predominantly in archaea and some bacteria, but also in plants and algae.
source: DNA topoisomerase VI (topo VI) is a type IIB DNA topoisomerase found predominantly in archaea and some bacteria, but also in plants and algae.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about topo VI that draws from established scientific knowledge about the distribution of this enzyme across different domains of life.

claim: Methanosarcina mazei topo VI preferentially unlinks, or decatenates DNA crossings, in comparison to relaxing supercoils, through a preference for certain DNA crossing geometries.
source: Using single-molecule magnetic tweezers measurements and supporting ensemble biochemistry, we demonstrate that Methanosarcina mazei topo VI preferentially unlinks, or decatenates DNA crossings, in comparison to relaxing supercoils, through a preference for certain DNA crossing geometries.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule magnetic tweezers measurements and ensemble biochemistry experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Topo VI demonstrates a significant increase in ATPase activity, DNA binding and rate of strand passage, with increasing DNA writhe.
source: In addition, topo VI demonstrates a significant increase in ATPase activity, DNA binding and rate of strand passage, with increasing DNA writhe, providing further evidence that topo VI is a DNA crossing sensor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays, DNA binding assays, and magnetic tweezers measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Topo VI has evolved an intrinsic preference for the unknotting and decatenation of interlinked chromosomes by sensing and preferentially unlinking DNA crossings with geometries close to 90°.
source: Our study strongly suggests that topo VI has evolved an intrinsic preference for the unknotting and decatenation of interlinked chromosomes by sensing and preferentially unlinking DNA crossings with geometries close to 90°.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing the preferred crossing angle and the implications for enzyme function.

claim: Type I topoisomerases utilize a transient single-stranded DNA break (SSB).
source: There are two topo families: the type I topos, which utilise a transient single-stranded DNA break (SSB), and the type II topos, which utilise a transient double-stranded DNA break (DSB) (McKie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about topoisomerase mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: Type II topoisomerases utilize a transient double-stranded DNA break (DSB).
source: There are two topo families: the type I topos, which utilise a transient single-stranded DNA break (SSB), and the type II topos, which utilise a transient double-stranded DNA break (DSB) (McKie et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about topoisomerase mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: Topoisomerases are vital during DNA metabolism, particularly in the relief of torsional stress built up ahead of and behind the transcription complexes and replication forks, as well as the removal of catenanes and knots.
source: These enzymes are vital during DNA metabolism, particularly in the relief of torsional stress built up ahead of and behind the transcription complexes and replication forks, as well as the removal of catenanes and knots (Bush et al., 2018; McKie et al., 2021; Pommier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing the biological roles of topoisomerases.

claim: Targeting topoisomerases as a means to treat bacterial infections and cancer has had significant and ongoing clinical success.
source: For this reason, targeting the topos as a means to treat bacterial infections and cancer has had significant and ongoing clinical success (Bush et al., 2020; Cuya et al., 2017; Hiasa, 2018; Pommier, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the clinical use of topoisomerase inhibitors.

claim: Type II topoisomerases are subcategorized as type IIA and type IIB based on structural and evolutionary premises.
source: The type II topos are further subcategorised as type IIA and type IIB (Gadelle et al., 2003). This separation is based on structural and evolutionary premises
evidence: This classification is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The general type II topoisomerase reaction, known as strand passage, is believed to be shared amongst all type II topoisomerases.
source: however, the general type II topo reaction, known as strand passage, is believed to be shared amongst all type II topos.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the conserved mechanism of type II topoisomerases.

claim: Strand passage involves the binding of one DNA duplex (G-segment), which is transiently cleaved and opened to allow the passage of a second DNA duplex (T-segment) through the break, thereby changing the topological state of the DNA.
source: Strand passage involves the binding of one DNA duplex, termed the gate segment (G-segment), which is transiently cleaved and opened to allow the passage of a second DNA duplex, the transported segment (T-segment), through the break, thereby changing the topological state of the DNA (Berger et al., 1996; Roca et al., 1996).
evidence: This mechanistic description is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All type II topoisomerases have been demonstrated to be active to some extent in both supercoil relaxation and decatenation reactions in vitro.
source: Even though all type II topos have been demonstrated to be active to some extent in both reactions in vitro (Bush et al., 2015), topos seemingly adopt preferential activities in vivo (McKie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work demonstrating the activities of type II topoisomerases.

claim: Topoisomerases seemingly adopt preferential activities in vivo.
source: Even though all type II topos have been demonstrated to be active to some extent in both reactions in vitro (Bush et al., 2015), topos seemingly adopt preferential activities in vivo (McKie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Escherichia coli DNA gyrase has been shown to be an integral component of the replication and transcriptional machinery.
source: Escherichia coli DNA gyrase (gyrase) has been shown to be an integral component of the replication and transcriptional machinery (Ahmed et al., 2017; Kreuzer and Cozzarelli, 1979; Stracy et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: E. coli DNA gyrase relieves torsional strain caused by positive supercoiling and allows fork progression.
source: relieving torsional strain caused by positive supercoiling and allowing fork progression (Khodursky et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli topoisomerase IV is indispensable for the decatenation of the replicated bacterial genome.
source: E. coli topoisomerase IV (topo IV), however, is indispensable for the decatenation of the replicated bacterial genome (Kato et al., 1990; Kato et al., 1988; Wang et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: E. coli topoisomerase IV exhibits highly processive and efficient relaxation of positive supercoils in vitro.
source: despite the highly processive and efficient relaxation of positive supercoils in vitro (Neuman et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: E. coli topoisomerase IV can, to an extent, support replication and transcription fork progression in vivo using cells encoding temperature-sensitive gyrase mutations.
source: and evidence that it can, to an extent, support replication and transcription fork progression in vivo using cells encoding temperature-sensitive gyrase mutations (Khodursky et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The preferential decatenation activity of topo IV in vivo is thought to be a consequence of protein-protein recruitment via the E. coli SMC complex, MukBEF, and temporal regulation.
source: The preferential decatenation activity of topo IV in vivo is thought to be a consequence of protein-protein recruitment via the E. coil SMC (structural maintenance of chromosome) complex, MukBEF (Hayama and Marians, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Nicolas et al., 2014; Nolivos et al., 2016), and temporal regulation (Espeli et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: DNA topoisomerase VI is a heterotetrameric, ATP/Mg2+-dependent type IIB topoisomerase formed from two Top6A and two Top6B subunits.
source: DNA topoisomerase VI (topo VI) is a heterotetrameric, ATP/Mg2+-dependent type IIB topo formed from two Top6A and two Top6B subunits, initially isolated from the hyperthermophillic archaeon, Sulfolobus shibatae in 1994 (Bergerat et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Topo VI was initially isolated from the hyperthermophilic archaeon, Sulfolobus shibatae in 1994.
source: DNA topoisomerase VI (topo VI) is a heterotetrameric, ATP/Mg2+-dependent type IIB topo formed from two Top6A and two Top6B subunits, initially isolated from the hyperthermophillic archaeon, Sulfolobus shibatae in 1994 (Bergerat et al., 1994).
evidence: This historical fact is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Topo VI is present throughout the archaeal domain, in some bacteria, and in certain eukaryotes, including plants and algae.
source: It was later demonstrated to be present throughout the archaeal domain, in some bacteria, and in certain eukaryotes, including plants and algae (Gadelle et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim about the distribution of topo VI is supported by a citation.

claim: The Top6A subunit is highly homologous to the eukaryotic meiotic factor, Spo11, crucial for the generation of DSBs during recombination.
source: The Top6A subunit is highly homologous to the eukaryotic meiotic factor, Spo11, crucial for the generation of DSBs during recombination (Claeys Bouuaert et al., 2021; Nichols et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim about structural homology and function is supported by citations.

claim: Top6B structural homologues have been identified in higher eukaryotes, including mouse and A. thaliana, and were shown to interact with Spo11.
source: Top6B structural homologues have also been identified in higher eukaryotes, including mouse and A. thaliana, and were shown to interact with Spo11 (Robert et al., 2016; Vrielynck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The purification of the Spo11 core complex was achieved, and structural data indicated a high degree of similarity to the topo VI heterotetramer.
source: Recently, the purification of the Spo11 core complex was achieved, and structural data indicated a high degree of similarity to the topo VI heterotetramer (Claeys Bouuaert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: S. shibatae topo VI was shown to relax positive and negative supercoils, but decatenated more efficiently, with threefold less enzyme required to decatenate 0.4 μg of kinetoplast DNA than was required to relax 0.4 μg of negatively supercoiled pTZ18.
source: S. shibatae topo VI was shown to relax positive and negative supercoils, but decatenated more efficiently, with threefold less enzyme required to decatenate 0.4 μg of kinetoplast (k)DNA than was required to relax 0.4 μg of negatively supercoiled pTZ18 (Bergerat et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A. thaliana topo VI was crucial during endoreduplication.
source: this result, along with the discovery that A. thaliana topo VI was crucial during endoreduplication (Hartung et al., 2002; Sugimoto-Shirasu et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Endoreduplication is a mechanism by which plant cells increase in size through multiple rounds of genome replication in the absence of mitosis.
source: a mechanism by which plant cells increase in size through multiple rounds of genome replication in the absence of mitosis (Sugimoto-Shirasu and Roberts, 2003)
evidence: This definitional statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Archaea encode topo III, known for its role in decatenation and DNA repair.
source: Exploring the phylogeny of archaeal topos revealed that archaea also encode topo III, known for its role in decatenation and DNA repair
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about topo III function.

claim: In Euryarchaeota and Crenarchaeota, topo VI was the only encoded topoisomerase capable of relaxing positive supercoils.
source: and that in Euryarchaeota and Crenarchaeota, topo VI was the only encoded topo capable of relaxing positive supercoils (Forterre and Gadelle, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both Methanosarcina mazei and S. shibatae full length topo VI have been characterized crystallographically, revealing an open and closed conformation, respectively.
source: Both Methanosarcina mazei (Corbett et al., 2007) and S. shibatae (Graille et al., 2008) full length topo VI have been characterised crystallographically, revealing an open and closed conformation, respectively, of a protein with a clamp-like structure forming an interior space large enough to accommodate two DNA duplexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Topo VI has a clamp-like structure forming an interior space large enough to accommodate two DNA duplexes.
source: Both Methanosarcina mazei (Corbett et al., 2007) and S. shibatae (Graille et al., 2008) full length topo VI have been characterised crystallographically, revealing an open and closed conformation, respectively, of a protein with a clamp-like structure forming an interior space large enough to accommodate two DNA duplexes.
evidence: This structural description is supported by citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: Top6A harbours the catalytic tyrosine and TOPRIM domain, the dimer of which constitutes a groove of the correct dimensions to bind the G-segment.
source: Top6A harbours the catalytic tyrosine and TOPRIM domain, the dimer of which constitutes a groove of the correct dimensions to bind the G-segment (Nichols et al., 1999).
evidence: This structural and functional description is supported by a citation.

claim: Top6B extends from the Top6A dimer to form a cavity that captures the T-segment.
source: Top6B extends from the Top6A dimer to form a cavity that captures the T-segment, and was demonstrated to be extremely important for tightly coupling ATPase activity to strand passage, indicating that topo VI senses and binds to DNA crossings and bends DNA (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
evidence: This structural and functional description is supported by a citation.

claim: Top6B was demonstrated to be extremely important for tightly coupling ATPase activity to strand passage.
source: Top6B extends from the Top6A dimer to form a cavity that captures the T-segment, and was demonstrated to be extremely important for tightly coupling ATPase activity to strand passage, indicating that topo VI senses and binds to DNA crossings and bends DNA (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
evidence: This functional claim is supported by a citation.

claim: M. mazei topo VI was an extremely slow and highly distributive supercoil relaxase.
source: This work also showed that M. mazei topo VI was an extremely slow and highly distributive supercoil relaxase.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Wendorff and Berger, 2018.

claim: At the rate measured using in vitro approaches, it is unlikely that topo VI functions fast enough to support replication and transcription within the host organism.
source: They calculated that at the rate measured using in vitro approaches, it is unlikely that the enzyme functions fast enough to support replication and transcription within the host organism.
evidence: This inference is based on calculations from previous work.

claim: Topo VI relaxed positive supercoils ~2–3 fold faster than negative supercoils.
source: The observed DNA extension changes revealed that, on average, topo VI relaxed positive supercoils ~2–3 fold faster than negative supercoils.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: The average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration.
source: We found that the average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration with the data fitted to a Michaelis Menten-like equation, resulting in an apparent Kd (Kd,app) threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: The apparent Kd for topo VI is threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe compared to negative.
source: We found that the average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration with the data fitted to a Michaelis Menten-like equation, resulting in an apparent Kd (Kd,app) threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements fitted to a Michaelis-Menten-like equation.

claim: The relaxation of positively and negatively supercoiled pBR322* by topo VI was completed by 6 min and 15 min, respectively.
source: In line with the single-molecule relaxation assay results, the preferential relaxation on positive supercoils by topo VI is also supported by an agarose gel based approach (Figure 1D), showing that the relaxation of positively and negatively supercoiled pBR322* was completed by 6 min and 15 min, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from an agarose gel-based assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each topo VI strand-passage event results in an abrupt DNA extension change of ∼100 nm, which corresponds to the resolution of a single DNA crossing.
source: For topo VI, each strand-passage event is evident in the trace, as an abrupt DNA extension change of ∼100 nm, which is expected for the resolution of a single DNA crossing (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Topo VI binds and resolves a single crossing before disengaging the G-segment, indicating distributive activity.
source: This provided preliminary evidence of distributive activity, as many seconds to minutes elapsed between strand-passage events, indicating that topo VI binds and resolves a single crossing before disengaging the G-segment.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation of long dwell times between strand-passage events in the magnetic tweezers data.

claim: The dwell time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship.
source: The dwell-time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship, indicating that the time taken to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The time taken for topo VI to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present.
source: The dwell-time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship, indicating that the time taken to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present (Figure 2C).
evidence: This inference is based on the inverse relationship fit to the experimental data.

claim: Topo VI specifically recognizes and binds DNA crossings, making each crossing along the plectoneme a potential site of activity.
source: This finding further supports the distributive nature of topo VI in supercoil relaxation and cements the conclusion described in Wendorff and Berger, 2018 that topo VI specifically recognises and binds DNA crossings (Wendorff and Berger, 2018), making each crossing along the plectoneme a potential site of activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work.

claim: Topo VI's specific binding to DNA crossings within the plectoneme is in sharp contrast to topo IV, which relaxed supercoiled DNA independent of the number of crossings.
source: This specific binding to DNA crossings within the plectoneme is in sharp contrast to topo IV, which relaxed supercoiled DNA independent of the number of crossings, suggesting a single binding site, hypothesised to be the plectoneme end-loop (Neuman et al., 2009).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and a citation to previous work on topo IV.

claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by topo VI was dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*.
source: Using a radioactive ATPase assay, the rate of ATP hydrolysis was observed to be dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*, and tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by topo VI is tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed.
source: Using a radioactive ATPase assay, the rate of ATP hydrolysis was observed to be dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*, and tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by topo VI with positively-supercoiled DNA was ~2 fold faster than with negatively-supercoiled DNA.
source: With positively-supercoiled DNA, we found that the rate of ATP hydrolysis, measured using a PK/LDH coupled assay, was ~2 fold faster than with negatively-supercoiled DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a PK/LDH coupled ATPase assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNA binding by topo VI in the absence of ATP increases with increasing levels of supercoiling.
source: DNA binding by topo VI in the absence of ATP, assayed using a nitrocellulose-membrane capture technique (Litwin et al., 2015), also indicates increased topo VI binding with increasing levels of supercoiling (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a nitrocellulose-membrane capture assay shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Topo VI preferentially bound negatively supercoiled DNA in the absence of ATP.
source: However, whereas relaxation and ATPase activity was ~2–3 fold higher for positive writhe than negative, topo VI preferentially bound negatively supercoiled DNA in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DNA binding assays.

claim: The topo VI preference for relaxing positive writhe may be facilitated during a stage post DNA binding, potentially DNA-gate opening or strand passage.
source: This suggested that the topo VI preference for relaxing positive writhe may be facilitated during a stage post DNA binding, potentially DNA-gate opening or strand passage.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that binding is higher for negative supercoils but relaxation is faster for positive supercoils.

claim: DNA cleavage by topo VI was enhanced on negatively-supercoiled DNA compared to positively-supercoiled DNA.
source: Furthermore, the amount of DNA cleavage, as measured using an agarose gel-based assay, also indicates that negatively-supercoiled DNA supports higher levels of ADPNP-dependent cleavage by topo VI than positively-supercoiled DNA (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from an agarose gel-based cleavage assay shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The maximum rate measured for positive and negative supercoil relaxation by topo VI was 6.4 ± 0.6 and 3.5 ± 0.5 strand-passage events min–1, respectively.
source: Even at high concentrations (e.g. 2 nM topo VI), the maximum rate measured for positive and negative supercoil relaxation was only 6.4 ± 0.6 and 3.5 ± 0.5 strand-passage events min–1, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: Topo VI supercoil relaxation rates are 10–50-fold slower than rates measured for the type IIA topoisomerases, gyrase and topo IV.
source: As detailed in the subsequent section, these rates are 10–50-fold slower than rates measured for the type IIA topos, gyrase and topo IV (Agarwal and Duderstadt, 2020; Basu et al., 2012; Stone et al., 2003).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and citations to previous work on other topoisomerases.

claim: The maximal topo VI ATP hydrolysis rate was ∼3 ATP min–1 during relaxation of negatively supercoiled plasmids.
source: Wendorff and Berger, 2018 found the maximal topo VI ATP hydrolysis rate, using the PK/LDH assay, to be ∼3 ATP min–1 during relaxation of negatively supercoiled plasmids (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The ATPase rate of topo VI was determined to be ∼5 ± 0.9 ATP min–1 using a radioactive ATPase assay.
source: Here, the ATPase rate was determined to be ∼5 ± 0.9 ATP min–1, using a radioactive ATPase assay (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The braid was relaxed by topo VI in three rapid bursts, at an average rate of ~0.5 strand-passage event s–1.
source: In Figure 4B, the example trace of braided DNA relaxation by 0.1 nM topo VI (0.5 pN), demonstrates that the braid was relaxed in three rapid bursts, at an average rate of ~0.5 strand-passage event s–1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The rate of braid unlinking by topo VI increased ~5 fold above that of supercoil relaxation.
source: however, even on average the rate of braid unlinking measured over a range of topo VI concentrations (0.05–0.9 nM) increased ~5 fold above that of supercoil relaxation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 0.5 nM topo VI relaxed positive supercoils at a rate of 3.5 ± 0.8 strand-passage events min–1, and positive braids at a rate of 18.9 ± 2.3 strand-passage events min–1.
source: For example, 0.5 nM topo VI relaxed positive supercoils at a rate of 3.5 ± 0.8 strand-passage events min–1, and positive braids at a rate of 18.9 ± 2.3 strand-passage events min–1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: Topo VI exhibited robust unlinking activity at concentrations ∼10-fold lower than was achievable in supercoil relaxation.
source: Moreover, topo VI exhibited robust unlinking activity at concentrations ∼10-fold lower than was achievable in supercoil relaxation, and with a limited processivity, passing consecutive T-segments while remaining bound to the initial G-segment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: Rates for topo VI processive activity approach ~0.8 strand-passage events s–1 on average during positive braid unlinking using 0.9 nM topo VI.
source: Rates for topo VI processive activity (dwell times between events not included in the average) approach ~0.8 strand-passage events s–1 on average (during positive braid unlinking using 0.9 nM topo VI) (Figure 4D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The processive rate of topo VI on braids is ~10 fold higher than the rate of positive supercoil relaxation at comparable topo VI concentrations.
source: which is ~10 fold higher than the rate of positive supercoil relaxation at comparable topo VI concentrations (~0.08 strand-passage events s–1 using 1 nM topo VI).
evidence: This comparison is based on experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: When topo VI activities were assayed using a singly-catenated, supercoiled DNA substrate, the decatenation reaction occurred at topo VI concentrations 10-fold lower than for supercoil relaxation.
source: In line with this, when topo VI activities were assayed using a singly-catenated, supercoiled DNA substrate, the decatenation reaction (Figure 5, left-hand agarose gel) occurred at topo VI concentrations 10-fold lower than for supercoil relaxation (Figure 5, right-hand agarose gel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from agarose gel-based assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The rate of braid unlinking by topo VI is on par with those of other type IIA topoisomerases on their preferred substrates.
source: Overall, the rate of braid unlinking by topo VI is on par with those of other type IIA topos on their preferred substrates.
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and citations to previous work on other topoisomerases.

claim: E. coli DNA gyrase showed one strand-passage event s–1 using a rotor bead tracking technique.
source: For instance, E. coli DNA gyrase, measured using a rotor bead tracking technique, showed one strand-passage event s–1 (Basu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli DNA gyrase showed 1.26 strand-passage events s–1 using magnetic tweezers.
source: or using magnetic tweezers, 1.26 strand-passage events s–1 (Agarwal and Duderstadt, 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: E. coli topo IV was demonstrated to relax positively supercoiled DNA at 2.5 strand-passage events s–1.
source: and E. coli topo IV was demonstrated to relax positively supercoiled DNA at 2.5 strand-passage events s–1 (Stone et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The average unlinking rates of topo VI at concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.9 nM were well described by a Michaelis-Menten-like equation, providing Vmax values of 21.4 ± 0.5 and 10.9 ± 1.3 strand-passage events min–1, and Kd,app of 67 ± 7 and 164 ± 72 pM, for the unlinking of positive and negative braids respectively.
source: The average unlinking rates (including dwell times between short processive bursts of activity) of topo VI at concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.9 nM were well described by a Michaelis-Menten-like equation, providing Vmax values of 21.4 ± 0.5 and 10.9 ± 1.3 strand-passage events min–1, and Kd,app of 67 ± 7 and 164 ± 72 pM, for the unlinking of positive and negative braids respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4C, fitted to a Michaelis-Menten-like equation.

claim: The Vmax for braid unlinking is ~2 fold higher, and the Kd,app ~2.5 fold lower, for positive-braid unlinking in comparison with negative.
source: The chiral preference remains, with the Vmax ~2 fold higher, and the Kd,app ~2.5 fold lower, for positive-braid unlinking in comparison with negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: The chiral selection by topo VI potentially occurs after G-segment binding and cleavage, during DNA-gate opening and/or strand passage.
source: Based on DNA binding and cleavage experiments (Figure 3C–E), the chiral selection potentially occurs after G-segment binding and cleavage as topo VI exhibits tighter binding and higher levels of cleavage in the presence of negative writhe than positive. This suggests that DNA-gate opening and/or strand passage is sensitive to the crossing angle, with a preference for angles more commonly found in positive writhe.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from DNA binding and cleavage assays shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The burst activity of topo VI on braids is due to processive unlinking by a single enzyme.
source: While the processive rate modestly increased over large changes in topo VI concentration (~1.5 fold increase for positive, ~2fold increase for negative) (Figure 4D), the size of the processive bursts remained constant (Figure 4E) and the duration of the dwell times between events decreased to a minimum (Figure 4F). Together these results support the hypothesis that the burst activity is due to processive unlinking by a single enzyme.
evidence: This inference is based on the concentration dependence of the processive rate, burst size, and dwell times shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: The experimental average step-sizes, probabilities of processive bursts, and average dwell times between relaxation events are substantially larger than the values from simulations of perfectly distributive braid relaxation.
source: The experimental average step-sizes, probabilities of processive bursts, and average dwell times between relaxation events, are substantially larger than the values from the simulations analysed in with the same t-test step fitting routine (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), consistent with a model in which topo VI relaxes braided DNA in short processive bursts between which the enzyme dissociates.
evidence: This comparison is based on experimental data and simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Topo VI does not bind well to the G-segment alone.
source: DNA binding and ATPase experiments show that topo VI inefficiently binds linear DNA, and the presence of this substrate does not greatly stimulate ATPase activity, indicating that topo VI does not bind well to the G-segment alone.
evidence: This inference is based on experimental data from DNA binding and ATPase assays.

claim: During the topo VI strand-passage reaction there is competition between the capture and passage of a T-segment at the correct geometry and the rate of topo VI dissociation from the DNA.
source: This suggests that during the topo VI strand-passage reaction there is competition between the capture and passage of a T-segment at the correct geometry and the rate of topo VI dissociation from the DNA, with the former likely being accelerated in the case of DNA braids.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in activity between braids and supercoils.

claim: DNA crossing-angles in braids were closer to 90° than those in supercoils.
source: Calculations of the average braid and supercoil angles as a function of force, corresponding to the experimental configurations of DNA length, buffer conditions, and spacing between braided DNA molecules, suggest that DNA crossing-angles in braids were closer to 90° than those in supercoils (Figure 6)
evidence: This claim is based on calculations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The DNA crossing angle may be the critical geometric factor promoting DNA unlinking by topo VI.
source: and that this may be the critical geometric factor promoting DNA unlinking by topo VI.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the calculated crossing angles and observed activity differences.

claim: With increasing force, the average rate of braid unlinking by topo VI drops significantly for both positive and negative writhe.
source: With increasing force, the average rate of braid unlinking drops significantly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), for both positive and negative writhe, mainly through an increase in dwell times between events with increasing force, although there is also a slight decrease in the rate and extent of the processive bursts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The supercoil relaxation rate of topo VI initially increased as the force was increased, but then rapidly decreased at higher forces.
source: This interpretation is bolstered by the supercoil relaxation rate of topo VI as a function of force; the rate initially increased as the force was increased, but then rapidly decreased at higher forces ( >1 pN for positive and >0.6 pN for negative).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claim: The characteristic unlinking time for positive crossings (τL) was 8.4 ± 1.4 s, which was 4.7-fold faster than that of negative crossings (τR) (43.8 ± 6.9 s).
source: In agreement with results from DNA braids and supercoils, the characteristic unlinking time from the fitting on positive crossings (τL) for the particular braid assayed in Figure 6 was 8.4 ± 1.4 s, which was 4.7-fold faster than that of negative crossings (τR) (43.8 ± 6.9 s), suggesting that a positive crossing geometry facilitates topo VI activity through the higher probability of forming the preferred crossing angle (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-crossing assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The preferred DNA-crossing angle for topo VI is 87.8° ± 0.4° when using Monte Carlo simulations, and 87.4° ± 0.4° when using Brownian Dynamics simulations.
source: Together these data indicate that the preferred DNA-crossing angle for topo VI is 87.8° ± 0.4°, when using MC simulations, and 87.4° ± 0.4° (uncertainties represent SEM), when using BD simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-crossing assays combined with Monte Carlo and Brownian Dynamics simulations.

claim: Combining the ATPase measurements of topo VI relaxing positively and negatively supercoiled DNA with crossing angle distributions of supercoiled plasmid DNA obtained from Monte Carlo simulations returns a preferred crossing angle in the range of 83° to 87°.
source: Furthermore, combining the ATPase measurements of topo VI relaxing positively and negatively supercoiled DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with crossing angle distributions of supercoiled plasmid DNA obtained from MC simulations performed by Vologodskii and Cozzarelli (Vologodskii and Cozzarelli, 1996; Vologodskii and Cozzarelli, 1994) permits an independent estimate of the preferred crossing angle of topo VI. This analysis returns a preferred crossing angle in the range of 83° to 87° (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), in excellent agreement with the value of 87.6° obtained from the more precise single molecule measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays combined with Monte Carlo simulations from previous work, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The preferred crossing angle for topo VI is similar to that found for topo IV, which was 85.5°.
source: The preferred crossing angle for topo VI is similar to that found for topo IV, attained using the same single-crossing assay, of 85.5° (Neuman et al., 2009).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and a citation to previous work on topo IV.

claim: The most acute imposed crossing angle (αL) that topo VI could unlink was 77°.
source: However, one distinct difference is that topo VI exhibited a far stricter preference for the DNA-crossing geometries on which it would act. If the imposed crossing angle (αL) is defined as the average angle in the positive distribution (see Figure 8A), then the most acute αL that topo VI could unlink was 77°, with no activity detected on braids with an αL lower than this (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-crossing assays shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Topo IV was able to unlink DNA-crossings with an imposed crossing angle (αL) as low as 50°.
source: However, topo IV seemed far more versatile and was able to unlink DNA-crossings with an αL as low as 50° (Neuman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on topo IV.

claim: M. mazei topo VI is a highly distributive and extremely slow supercoil relaxase.
source: Using the magnetic tweezers single-molecule approach, we have not only demonstrated that M. mazei topo VI is a highly distributive and extremely slow supercoil relaxase, confirming findings from Wendorff and Berger, 2018 (Wendorff and Berger, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work.

claim: Topo VI activity increases as much as ~10 fold on braided DNA compared to supercoiled DNA.
source: but have also shown that topo VI activity increases as much as ~10 fold on braided DNA, (Figures 1, 2 and 4), approaching rates determined for type IIA topos on their respective optimal substrates (Agarwal and Duderstadt, 2020; Basu et al., 2012; Stone et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Topo VI has an extremely strict preference for DNA crossing geometries close to 90°, which appear more frequently in catenanes than they do in supercoils.
source: Along with the observation that topo VI has an extremely strict preference for DNA crossing geometries close to 90°, which appear more frequently in catenanes than they do in supercoils (Stone et al., 2003), these data strongly indicate that M. mazei topo VI is a preferential decatenase, which simultaneously disfavours supercoil relaxation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work on crossing angle distributions.

claim: M. mazei topo VI is a preferential decatenase, which simultaneously disfavours supercoil relaxation.
source: these data strongly indicate that M. mazei topo VI is a preferential decatenase, which simultaneously disfavours supercoil relaxation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The 2–3-fold increase in topo VI activity on positive writhe was not particularly large, unlike the difference seen for topo IV, which relaxed positive writhe ~20 fold faster than negative.
source: While significant, with both supercoiled and braided DNA substrates, the 2–3-fold increase in rate on positive writhe was not particularly large, unlike the difference seen for topo IV, which relaxed positive writhe ~20 fold faster than negative (Neuman et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2003).
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and citations to previous work on topo IV.

claim: M. mazei encodes a DNA gyrase, which maintains the genome in a negatively supercoiled state.
source: However, as M. mazei encodes a DNA gyrase, which maintains the genome in a negatively supercoiled state, the slight preference for positive DNA crossings may prevent topo VI from interfering with the activity of DNA gyrase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA gyrase function.

claim: The slight preference of topo VI for positive DNA crossings may prevent topo VI from interfering with the activity of DNA gyrase.
source: However, as M. mazei encodes a DNA gyrase, which maintains the genome in a negatively supercoiled state, the slight preference for positive DNA crossings may prevent topo VI from interfering with the activity of DNA gyrase.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential in vivo implications of the observed chiral preference.

claim: Topo VI can help support the relief of replication- and transcription-induced torsional strain in combination with other topoisomerases.
source: It may also indicate, as supercoils ahead of replication forks are positive, that topo VI can help support the relief of replication- and transcription-induced torsional strain in combination with other topos.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential in vivo role of topo VI.

claim: Chiral selection by topo VI does not occur at the initial DNA binding step.
source: Binding experiments in the absence of ATP indicate that negative DNA crossings are bound more tightly than positive (Figure 3C and D), despite both single-molecule and ensemble measurements revealing a two- to threefold rate enhancement in the presence of positive writhe (Figures 1C—4). This suggests that chiral selection does not occur at the initial DNA binding step.
evidence: This inference is based on experimental data from DNA binding and activity assays.

claim: Topo VI is a DNA-crossing sensor, binding the G- and T-segments simultaneously, rather than binding a G-segment first before capturing a T-segment.
source: In addition, further confirming observations by Wendorff and Berger, 2018, data reported here suggest that topo VI is a DNA-crossing sensor (Wendorff and Berger, 2018), e.g. binding the G- and T-segments simultaneously, rather than binding a G-segment first before capturing a T-segment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work.

claim: Strand-passage by topo VI occurs more quickly in plectonemes with more DNA crossings.
source: This model of topo VI is supported by data showing that strand-passage occurs more quickly in plectonemes with more DNA crossings (Figure 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by topo VI is tightly coupled to the presence of DNA writhe.
source: the rate of ATP hydrolysis is tightly coupled to the presence of DNA writhe (Figure 3A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: DNA binding by topo VI increases with increasing supercoil density.
source: and DNA binding increases with increasing supercoil density (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DNA binding assays shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Domains within the Top6B subunit are critical to recognizing the T-segment and coupling this to G-segment scission.
source: It is known from work done by Wendorff and Berger that domains within the Top6B subunit are critical to recognising the T-segment and coupling this to G-segment scission (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Topo VI's preference for relaxing positive writhe may occur at a stage post DNA binding and cleavage, potentially DNA-gate opening and/or strand-passage.
source: This leaves DNA-gate opening and strand passage as the most likely candidates for the chiral discrimination step.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that binding and cleavage are enhanced for negative supercoils.

claim: The structure of the open DNA-gate of topo IIβ revealed that the T-segment would likely need to transfer through the break in the left-handed orientation.
source: There is precedence for this interpretation based on the structure of the type IIA topo, topo IIβ (Chen et al., 2018). The structure of the open DNA-gate of topo IIβ, with a fully cleaved and separated G-segment, revealed that the T-segment would likely need to transfer through the break in the left-handed orientation and was suggested to provide further rationale for the type IIA preference for positive-DNA crossings.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a structural study.

claim: The switch from highly distributive topo VI activity in the presence of supercoils to mild processivity on braids is likely due to the DNA-crossing geometries found in braids promoting more efficient strand-capture and passage.
source: There are two main differences between the magnetic tweezers supercoiling and braiding substrates: (1) braids do not accumulate twist upon magnet rotation, while supercoils do, and (2) the DNA crossing angle geometries of braids are closer to 90° than those within the plectoneme (Figure 6). So it is likely that one factor, or a combination of both, promotes the processive unlinking of braided DNA substrates by topo VI. The latter is the more likely candidate, with the DNA-crossing geometries found in braids potentially promoting more efficient strand-capture and passage due to the larger imposed crossing angles (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in activity and the calculated crossing angles shown in Figure 6.

claim: After the initial strand passage there is a kinetic competition between topo VI releasing the G-segment versus capturing a T-segment and catalyzing another strand passage cycle.
source: After the initial strand passage there is a kinetic competition between topo VI releasing the G-segment versus capturing a T-segment and catalysing another strand passage cycle.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the observed processivity on braids.

claim: The larger crossing angles in braids facilitate T-segment capture, resulting in an increase in the number of strand passages catalyzed before topo VI releases the G-segment.
source: The larger crossing angles in braids facilitate T-segment capture, resulting in an increase in the number of strand passages catalysed before topo VI releases the G-segment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed processivity on braids and the calculated crossing angles.

claim: At low force (0.4 pN), the increase in twist is minimal as the plectoneme forms after 3–4 magnet rotations.
source: At low force, which was utilised in the supercoil relaxation measurements (0.4 pN), the increase in twist is minimal as the plectoneme forms after 3–4 magnet rotations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on the calibration data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A minor change in twist is unlikely to be responsible for the significantly decreased activity of topo VI on supercoils in comparison to braids.
source: Therefore, it seems unlikely that a minor change in twist would be responsible for the significantly decreased activity on supercoils in comparison to braids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that twist changes are minimal at low force.

claim: Supercoil relaxation rate by topo VI initially increased as force, and twist, increased.
source: In addition, supercoil relaxation rate initially increased as force, and twist, increased (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Twist may become important at higher forces in determining topo VI activity, but this appears to be a secondary factor.
source: The relaxation rate subsequently decreased as the force increased, indicating that twist may become important at higher forces, but this appears to be a secondary factor in determining strand passage rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the force-dependent activity data.

claim: Increasing the force on the DNA braid reduced the strand-passage rate by topo VI, largely due to increasing dwell times between catalytic events.
source: Moreover, increasing the force on the DNA braid reduced the strand-passage rate, largely due to increasing dwell times between catalytic events, but also decreasing both the processive rate and the number of strand passages per processive burst (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: As force increases on braids, the average braid angles deviate further from 90°.
source: As force increases, the average braid angles deviate further from 90° (Figure 6), and distributions likely narrow, meaning the probability of achieving the topo VI preferred crossing angle will also decrease.
evidence: This claim is based on calculations shown in Figure 6.

claim: For processivity to occur, topo VI must remain bound to the initial G-segment once the T-segment has passed.
source: However, for processivity to occur, topo VI must remain bound to the initial G-segment once the T-segment has passed.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for processive activity.

claim: The initial increase in supercoil relaxation rate with increasing force can be explained by the average supercoil angles becoming closer to 90° as force increases.
source: The initial increase in rate can be explained by the average supercoil angles becoming closer to 90° as force increases (Figure 6).
evidence: This inference is based on the calculated crossing angles shown in Figure 6 and the observed force-dependent activity.

claim: The significant decrease in supercoil relaxation rate at high force could be due to changes in twist preventing DNA binding or cleavage.
source: The significant decrease in rate that occurs at high force, however, could be due to changes in twist preventing DNA binding or cleavage.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the cause of the decreased activity at high force.

claim: The significant decrease in supercoil relaxation rate at high force could be due to inhibition of a step that is directly sensitive to force, such as G-segment binding or cleavage, or gate closure.
source: However, this could also be due to inhibition of a step that is directly sensitive to force, such as G-segment binding or cleavage, which induce bending of the DNA, or gate closure, particularly since the twist increases sub-linearly with increasing force.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the cause of the decreased activity at high force.

claim: Archaea constitute the third domain of the tree of life, alongside bacteria and eukarya.
source: Archaea constitute the third domain of the tree of life, alongside bacteria and eukarya.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the classification of life.

claim: Archaea were distinguished from bacteria based on their unique ribosomal proteins and RNA.
source: Archaea were distinguished from bacteria, previously having been grouped together, based on their unique ribosomal proteins and RNA (Forterre et al., 2002).
evidence: This historical fact is supported by a citation.

claim: Like bacteria, archaea have sequence-specific origins of replication and encode transcriptional regulators that resemble those found in bacteria.
source: For instance, like bacteria, archaea have sequence-specific origins of replication and encode transcriptional regulators that resemble those found in bacteria (Ausiannikava and Allers, 2017; Bell and Jackson, 2001).

claim: Like the eukarya, archaea utilize a basal transcriptional complex that resembles the eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, can have multiple origins of replication, and many species compact their genomes through the use of histone-like proteins.

claim: Almost all archaea contain topo VI, aside from the order Thermoplasmatales, which instead encodes a DNA gyrase.
source: Almost all archaea contain topo VI, aside from the order Thermoplasmatales, which instead encodes a DNA gyrase, whereas some, including the Methanosarcina order, encode both gyrase and topo VI (Forterre and Gadelle, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some archaea, including the Methanosarcina order, encode both gyrase and topo VI.
source: Almost all archaea contain topo VI, aside from the order Thermoplasmatales, which instead encodes a DNA gyrase, whereas some, including the Methanosarcina order, encode both gyrase and topo VI (Forterre and Gadelle, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: All archaea, aside from the Thaumarchaea, encode one or more copies of a type IA topoisomerase, which resembles bacterial and eukaryotic topo III.
source: In addition to type II topos, all archaea, aside from the Thuamarchaea, encode one or more copies of a type IA topo, which, in terms of sequence similarity, resembles bacterial and eukaryotic topo III, as opposed to bacterial topo IA (Forterre et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Topo VI must be involved in the removal of positive supercoils during transcription and replication, particularly in archaea lacking a gyrase, as topo III is a preferential decatenase.
source: This has led to the proposal that topo VI must be involved in the removal of positive supercoils during transcription and replication, particularly in archaea lacking a gyrase, as topo III is a preferential decatenase (Lee et al., 2019).

claim: M. mazei topo VI is an extremely inefficient DNA relaxase.
source: However, the work reported here solidifies the observation by Wendorff and Berger, 2018 (Wendorff and Berger, 2018), that M. mazei topo VI is an extremely inefficient DNA relaxase, and provides evidence of its preferential decatenation activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work.

claim: If topo VI behavior is true of all archaeal topo VI enzymes, then organisms that lack DNA gyrase would struggle to relieve torsional stress ahead of replication forks at a pace required by the cell, if they also do not have an efficient type I relaxase capable of relaxing positive supercoils.
source: If this behaviour is true of all archaeal topo VI enzymes, then those organisms that lack DNA gyrase, would struggle to relieve torsional stress ahead of replication forks at a pace required by the cell, if they also do not have an efficient type I relaxase capable of relaxing positive supercoils, like a type IB.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the implications of the findings for archaeal biology.

claim: The first archaeal type IA topoisomerase explored in vitro, from Desulfurococcus amylolyticus, exhibited robust relaxation activity of both positive and negative writhe at 95 °C.
source: The current literature confounds the issue as the first archaeal type IA topo explored in vitro, from the hyperthermophile Desulfurococcus amylolyticus, also termed topo III, was claimed to exhibit robust relaxation activity of both positive and negative writhe at 95 °C.
evidence: This claim is based on previous literature, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: In Sulfolobus solfataricus, two of the three type IA topoisomerases it encodes are reverse gyrases, and the third is topo III, exhibiting preferential decatenation activity.
source: However, it has also been established in Sulfolobus solfataricus, that of the three type IA topos it encodes, two are reverse gyrases (Bizard et al., 2011) (another type IA topo important in positive supercoiling of hyperthermophillic genomes) (Nadal, 2007), and the third is topo III, exhibiting preferential decatenation activity (Bizard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In archaea that lack DNA gyrase and are apparently devoid of a type IA relaxase, topo VI may have evolved more efficient DNA relaxation activity.
source: It may be that in archaea that lack DNA gyrase and are apparently devoid of a type IA relaxase, that topo VI has evolved more efficient DNA relaxation activity, similar to how Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA gyrase has evolved to efficiently both supercoil and decatenate DNA in the absence of topo IV (Manjunatha et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation to an analogous example.

claim: M. mazei encodes both topo VI and DNA gyrase, as well as two uncharacterized type IA topoisomerases.
source: M. mazei encodes both topo VI and DNA gyrase, as well as two uncharacterised type IA topos, meaning that topo VI may not be required during positive supercoil relaxation and hence has evolved to preferentially decatenate.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic content of M. mazei.

claim: The slow relaxation by topo VI may be adequate to support the growth of some archaea, which did not seem to be the case for M. mazei.
source: It is also important, as was done in Wendorff and Berger, 2018, to consider the doubling time of the archaea in question, as the slow relaxation by topo VI may be adequate to support the growth of that particular organism, which did not seem to be the case for M. mazei (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Topo VI's main in vivo role could be precatenane removal, which may occur closer to the termination of replication, or even during elongation or at cell division.
source: In addition, topo VI's main in vivo role could be precatenane removal, which may occur closer to the termination of replication, or even during elongation or at cell division.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential in vivo role of topo VI.

claim: If the replication fork can swivel in vivo, positive supercoiling generated ahead of polymerase may be redistributed to form precatenanes behind the fork in archaea.
source: For instance, if the replication fork can swivel in vivo, which is known to occur in bacteria and eukaryotes (Cebrián et al., 2015; Schalbetter et al., 2015), positive supercoiling generated ahead of polymerase may be redistributed to form precatenanes behind the fork in archaea, which are likely a preferred topo VI substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to previous work on fork swiveling in other organisms.

claim: In cells seemingly devoid of an efficient relaxase, topo VI may be able to efficiently support fork progression through unlinking of precatenated DNA, rather than relaxation of supercoils.
source: Therefore, in cells seemingly devoid of an efficient relaxase, topo VI may be able to efficiently support fork progression through unlinking of precatenated DNA, rather than relaxation of supercoils.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential in vivo role of topo VI.

claim: Topo VI exhibits partially processive behavior, which may provide a functional explanation for its role in the rapid removal of precatenanes.
source: This may also provide a functional explanation for why topo VI exhibits partially processive behaviour, as this would have utility in the rapid removal of precatenanes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional significance of the observed processivity.

claim: Topo VI preferentially unlinks rather than relaxes singly-catenated negatively supercoiled substrates, in line with its preference for a crossing angle near 90°.
source: Although topo VI preferentially unlinks rather than relaxes singly-catenated negatively supercoiled substrates (Figure 5), in line with its preference for a crossing angle near 90°
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The crossing angle distribution in catenated DNA molecules depends on both the sign and extent of supercoiling.
source: the crossing angle distribution in catenated DNA molecules depends on both the sign and extent of supercoiling (Vologodskii and Cozzarelli, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Homozygous null mutations in either AtSPO11-3 or AtTOP6B in A. thaliana displayed identical phenotypes with severely growth stunted plants that failed to thrive.
source: Genomic analysis of Arabidopsis thaliana revealed that the Topo6A (AtSPO11-3) and Topo6B (AtTOP6B) genes were encoded, and homozygous null mutations in either, displayed identical phenotypes with severely growth stunted plants that failed to thrive (Hartung et al., 2002; Hartung and Puchta, 2000; Hartung and Puchta, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Double mutants of AtSPO11-3 and AtTOP6B displayed a phenotype identical to that of either single mutant, demonstrating the proteins likely function in the same process, or even the same protein complex.
source: Furthermore, double mutants displayed a phenotype identical to that of either single mutant, demonstrating the proteins likely function in the same process, or even the same protein complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic data from previous work.

claim: Endoreduplication was shown to be deficient in the AtSPO11-3/AtTOP6B mutants and explained the dwarf phenotype.
source: A process called endoreduplication, in which the genome is replicated multiple times in the absence of cellular division, is critical for plant growth to enlarge hypocotyl and leaf cells (Sugimoto-Shirasu and Roberts, 2003), was shown to be deficient in the AtSPO11-3/AtTOP6B mutants and explained the dwarf phenotype (Robert et al., 2016; Vrielynck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A. thaliana possesses four type I topoisomerases, along with topo II and DNA gyrase, both of which are type IIA topoisomerases capable of DNA decatenation, unknotting, and relaxation.
source: However, A. thaliana possesses four type I topos, along with topo II and DNA gyrase, both of which are type IIA topos capable of the same reactions as topo VI, namely DNA decatenation, unknotting, and relaxation (Corbett and Berger, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: During the endocycle in wild-type A. thaliana trichomes, the genome can be replicated to as high as 32 C.
source: During the endocycle, the genome is replicated to variable degrees, however in wild-type A. thaliana trichomes this can be as high as 32 C (Sugimoto-Shirasu and Roberts, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutants in topo VI are unable to replicate the genome past 8 C during endoreduplication.
source: with mutants in topo VI unable to replicate the genome past 8 C (Hartung et al., 2002; Sugimoto-Shirasu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Type I and type IIA topoisomerases are very efficient at relaxation, and may become subsumed by the necessity to relieve torsional stress generated ahead of replication and transcription forks during endoreduplication.
source: It is possible, therefore, as these proteins are very efficient at relaxation, that even though they are known to efficiently decatenate in vitro, they become subsumed by the necessity to relieve torsional stress generated ahead of replication and transcription forks.

claim: With relaxation so heavily disfavored by topo VI, it could decatenate and unknot the genome unhindered during endoreduplication, allowing the cell to continue through the endocycle.

claim: The research does not rule out the possibility of protein-protein recruitment, temporal regulation, or other activity-modulating factors which lead to the indispensability of topo VI in endoreduplication.
source: The research described here, clearly does not rule out the possibility of protein-protein recruitment, temporal regulation, or other activity-modulating factors which lead to the indispensability of topo VI in endoreduplication, but does provide a rationale that is independent of the requirement of these yet unknown components.
